questions.text: A student looks at two unlabelled microscope slides — one is a cheek cell from a human, the other is from an onion epidermis. Which combination of features would let them confirm the onion cell?
options: Has a cell membrane and nucleus only
Has a rigid cell wall, a large central vacuole, and a regular rectangular shape
Contains chloroplasts and is spherical
Has many mitochondria but no nucleus
questions.expectedAnswer: Has a rigid cell wall, a large central vacuole, and a regular rectangular shape
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer describes the cell wall, large vacuole and rectangular shape.

Here's why:
Both plant and animal cells have cell membranes, nuclei and mitochondria, so those are not distinguishing features.
Onion epidermis cells are NOT photosynthetic so they don't have chloroplasts (a common trap).
The rigid cellulose cell wall and the large central vacuole are unique to plant cells, and the rigid wall gives onion cells their characteristic 'brick' shape.
Exam tip: 'plant cell = chloroplasts' is only true for cells in green tissue. Always think about the function of the cell.

questions.text:
A student grows two pea plants. Plant A is in a sealed greenhouse kept at a constant 35 °C with bright light. Plant B is kept at 22 °C with the same bright light. Plant A grows much more SLOWLY than Plant B even though it has more 'tropical' conditions.

Which is the BEST explanation?
options: At 35 °C the enzymes in photosynthesis begin to denature, so the rate of photosynthesis falls and the plant produces less glucose
Plants only photosynthesise at night, so the bright light damaged the plant
Plant A is warmer so it doesn't need to grow
Plant A used up all the oxygen in the greenhouse and died
questions.expectedAnswer: At 35 °C the enzymes in photosynthesis begin to denature, so the rate of photosynthesis falls and the plant produces less glucose
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is the enzyme denaturation explanation.

Here's why:
Photosynthesis is controlled by enzymes, which work best at an optimum temperature (around 25 °C for many plants).
At very high temperatures (around 35 °C and above), the enzymes start to lose their shape (denature), so the rate of photosynthesis drops sharply.
Plants take in CO2 and release O2 during the day, so 'used up all the oxygen' is wrong.
Exam tip: enzyme + temperature is a classic Year 10 application.

questions.text: A normal human body cell contains 46 chromosomes. A sperm cell is produced by meiosis. Which row CORRECTLY describes the sperm cell and the cell formed when it fuses with an egg at fertilisation?
options: Sperm: 23 chromosomes, fertilised cell: 46 chromosomes
Sperm: 46 chromosomes, fertilised cell: 92 chromosomes
Sperm: 23 chromosomes, fertilised cell: 23 chromosomes
Sperm: 46 chromosomes, fertilised cell: 46 chromosomes
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is sperm 23, fertilised cell 46.

Here's why:
Meiosis halves the chromosome number, so a sperm (or egg) carries 23 chromosomes — half of the body cell's 46.
When sperm and egg fuse, the chromosomes combine: 23 + 23 = 46, returning to the normal body-cell number.
This is how each parent contributes half of the offspring's genetic information.
Exam tip: gametes (sex cells) are HAPLOID (n=23), body cells are DIPLOID (2n=46).

questions.text:
Two parents both have brown eyes but their child has blue eyes. The brown allele (B) is dominant and the blue allele (b) is recessive.

What are the parents' genotypes, and what is the chance their next child will also have blue eyes?
options: Both parents are BB; 0% chance
Both parents are Bb; 25% chance
Both parents are bb; 100% chance
One parent BB, the other Bb; 50% chance
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is both Bb, 25%.

Here's why:
For a child to have blue eyes (bb), they must inherit a 'b' from each parent.
Both parents have brown eyes but produced a blue-eyed child, so they must each carry a hidden 'b' — they are heterozygous (Bb).
A Bb × Bb cross gives a Punnett square with offspring 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb, so 1 in 4 (25%) are blue-eyed.
Exam tip: hidden recessive alleles are a classic Year 10 / Level 5 question.

questions.text:
In the food chain: phytoplankton → krill → blue cod → bottlenose dolphin

A disease causes a sudden 90% drop in the krill population. Which prediction BEST describes the SHORT-TERM and LONG-TERM consequences?
options: Short term: blue cod numbers fall as their food runs out. Long term: dolphin numbers also fall, and phytoplankton may bloom because fewer krill graze on them
Short term: blue cod numbers rise because there is less competition for space. Long term: dolphins increase
Nothing changes because the food chain is fixed
Phytoplankton numbers crash immediately because they depend on krill for food
questions.expectedAnswer: Short term: blue cod numbers fall as their food runs out. Long term: dolphin numbers also fall, and phytoplankton may bloom because fewer krill graze on them
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is the short/long-term cascade option.

Here's why:
Krill are the food source for blue cod, so blue cod will starve and decline (short term).
With fewer blue cod, dolphins also have less food and decline (long term).
With fewer krill grazing, phytoplankton populations can increase rapidly (a knock-on bottom-up effect).
This demonstrates how disturbance at one trophic level can cascade up AND down the food chain.
Exam tip: phytoplankton are the producers — they use sunlight, not krill.

questions.text: The small intestine is the main site of nutrient absorption in the human digestive system. Describe TWO specific structural adaptations of the small intestine, and for EACH adaptation explain how it makes absorption more efficient.
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark per adaptation IF the answer includes BOTH the structure AND a clear explanation of how it helps absorption. 2 required.

Examples of strong answers:

Villi (and microvilli): the inner wall is folded into thousands of finger-like villi covered in even smaller microvilli. This massively increases the surface area available for nutrients to be absorbed into the blood. (Up to 200 m² in an adult.)

Thin walls (one cell thick): the wall of each villus is only one cell thick, so nutrients have a very short distance to diffuse from the gut into the blood capillaries.

Rich blood supply: each villus contains a network of capillaries that constantly carries away absorbed nutrients, maintaining a steep concentration gradient so absorption can continue.

Long length (around 6 m): the long tube means food spends more time in contact with the absorbing surface.

Do not award the second mark for only naming a structure with no explanation.

questions.text: Explain how the circulatory and respiratory systems work TOGETHER to supply a working leg muscle with oxygen during a sprint, and to remove the carbon dioxide produced. In your answer use the words: alveoli, capillaries, diffusion, heart, arteries, veins.
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark for explaining gas exchange at the lungs: oxygen breathed into the lungs DIFFUSES from the ALVEOLI into the surrounding CAPILLARIES (because oxygen is at a higher concentration in the alveoli). Carbon dioxide diffuses the other way and is breathed out.

1 mark for explaining transport to the muscle: the HEART pumps oxygen-rich blood through ARTERIES to the leg muscle, where oxygen DIFFUSES out of the capillaries into the muscle cells (used in respiration to release energy from glucose). CO2 produced in the muscle diffuses into the blood and returns to the heart via the VEINS, then back to the lungs to be exhaled.

Key concept (must be present): diffusion always happens from HIGH to LOW concentration.

Deduct a mark if the student does not use most of the listed scientific terms or confuses arteries and veins.

questions.text:
An island has a simple food web: native trees (producers) → wētā and kererū (primary consumers) → ruru/morepork (secondary consumer). Stoats are introduced.

Explain in detail why introducing stoats is so damaging to this food web. In your answer you must:
• describe the impact on TWO different native species
• explain ONE knock-on effect on the wider ecosystem (e.g. plants, soil)
• use the term 'evolved without mammalian predators'.
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: Explains that NZ native species EVOLVED WITHOUT MAMMALIAN PREDATORS, so they have few defences against fast climbing/digging mammals like stoats. Stoats are also a 'new' predator at multiple trophic levels (eating both primary and secondary consumers).

1 mark: Specific impact on TWO native species. Examples:

Kererū — slow, fearless, ground-feeding birds that are easy prey; their populations fall.

Wētā — large, ground-dwelling and active at night, exactly when stoats hunt; populations crash.

Ruru — stoats raid nests and eat eggs/chicks, reducing breeding success.

1 mark: Knock-on ecosystem effect. Examples:

Kererū are the only NZ native birds large enough to swallow and disperse the seeds of taraire, karaka and miro. Without them, those native trees can no longer regenerate, slowly changing the forest composition.

Loss of wētā affects nutrient cycling and removes a major food source for other native species.

Loss of ruru reduces top-down control of insect populations.

Exam tip: Year 10 / Level 5 ecology questions reward students who can describe a CHAIN of consequences, not just one impact.

questions.text:
The Predator Free 2050 initiative aims to remove rats, stoats, and possums from New Zealand by 2050.

Explain why this programme is important for NZ's native biodiversity. In your answer you MUST include:
• ONE specific native species that would benefit AND a measurable statistic about how it is affected by predators
• how removing predators would help that species recover
• ONE realistic scientific or social challenge in achieving the goal, with a brief explanation of why it is a challenge
• at least TWO of these scientific terms used correctly: biodiversity, ecosystem, endemic, kaitiakitanga, eradication.
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: Names a specific native species AND gives a credible statistic. Examples:

Kiwi — only about 5% of kiwi chicks reach adulthood in unmanaged areas because of stoat predation.

Kākāpō — total population dropped to 51 in 1995, recovering to over 200 today only because of intensive predator control on offshore islands.

Mohua/yellowhead, whio (blue duck), tuatara are all acceptable.

1 mark: Explains how removing predators helps recovery — e.g. without stoats, kiwi chick survival jumps dramatically; in fenced sanctuaries like Zealandia and Maungatautari, native bird and reptile populations recover and forest ecosystems rebound.

1 mark: Identifies a realistic challenge AND explains WHY it is a challenge. Examples:

Reinvasion — even after eradication, predators can swim or be transported back from surrounding areas, so ongoing biosecurity is needed.

Scale and cost — NZ is large and rugged, so the project will cost billions; sustained funding over 25+ years is politically difficult.

Developing species-specific tools — current toxins like 1080 also affect some non-target species and are controversial with the public, so new methods are needed.

1 mark: Quality of explanation — links ideas logically and uses AT LEAST TWO of the listed scientific/Māori terms correctly (biodiversity, ecosystem, endemic, kaitiakitanga, eradication).

Exam tip: Excellence answers don't just LIST facts, they EXPLAIN the chain of cause and effect.

questions.text:
A scientist studying the Hauraki Gulf marine ecosystem notices that overfishing of snapper has led to an increase in kina (sea urchin) populations. The kina graze large areas of kelp, creating 'kina barrens'.

The graph above shows estimated population changes between 1990 and 2020.

(a) Calculate the percentage decrease in kelp cover from 1990 to 2020. Show your working.
(b) Calculate the average rate of change in kina population per year between 1990 and 2020 (in index points per year).
(c) Using your knowledge of food webs, explain in detail how the removal of one species (snapper) led to such a large change in the ecosystem. Use the term 'trophic cascade' and predict what would happen if snapper were allowed to recover.

graph.title: Estimated Population Trends in the Hauraki Gulf (1990–2020)

questions.markingGuide:
1 mark (a): Kelp dropped from 90 (1990) to 15 (2020). Decrease = 75. Percentage decrease = (75/90) × 100 = 83.3%. Accept 83% or 83.3% with working shown.

1 mark (b): Kina rose from 20 (1990) to 90 (2020) over 30 years. Change = 70 index points. Rate = 70 / 30 ≈ 2.33 index points per year. Accept 2.3 to 2.4 with working.

1 mark (c) trophic cascade: snapper are a key predator of kina. Overfishing removes the top-down control on kina. Kina populations explode and overgraze the kelp forest, removing critical habitat and reducing biodiversity (creates 'kina barrens'). The student must use the term 'trophic cascade'.

1 mark (c) recovery prediction + quality: if snapper are protected and rebuild, they will eat more kina, kina numbers will fall, kelp can regrow, and biodiversity in the Gulf can recover. Quality of scientific reasoning — uses terms like trophic cascade, top-down control, keystone species, biodiversity, ecosystem.

Exam tip: This is a real example from Auckland's Hauraki Gulf — a great connection between Year 10 ecology and current NZ marine science.
